title: Replace a damaged brick in a wall, bedded in mortar
instruction: Replace the damaged brick: clear the broken pieces out of the pocket into the bucket, spread the mortar on the trowel over the pocket's bed, then set the brick that matches the wall on the bed, flush with the wall face.
context: Laying a brick in mortar is one of the most recognisable trades: most people have watched a mason spread a bed with a trowel and set a brick into line. Brick is the main outside wall of about 33 million US homes, more than a quarter of them (EIA RECS 2020), and replacing a cracked or spalled brick is a common repair on houses, garden walls and chimneys. Here the damaged brick and its mortar are already cut out. The robot clears the debris, spreads a full bed of mortar with a trowel inside the narrow pocket under the course above, and sets a 1.9 kg brick two-handed into an opening only 2 cm longer and taller than the brick, flush and level. The head and top joints are packed afterwards (not part of this task).
setup: Dream Labs' YAM station (scene=station), both arms starting at their ready pose. World frame: origin between the arm bases, x forward, y to the left, z up; the table top is at z = 0.7475 m. Everything is fixed (for real trials, clamp or tape the bankers, mortar board, trowel block and bucket to the table) except the two broken pieces, the two loose bricks and the trowel. Wall: a solid brick wall two bricks thick, 60.2 cm long (y -0.301 to 0.301 m) and 39.2 cm high, its face toward the arms at x 0.48 m. Its outer layer is six courses of red US modular face brick (194 x 92 x 57 mm, sRGB 0.62, 0.25, 0.18) in running bond with 10 mm grey mortar joints (sRGB 0.72, 0.70, 0.65) tooled 4 mm back from the face; behind it, an inner layer of brick 10.2 cm thick (x 0.572 to 0.674 m). For real trials, build the wall once with mortar on a plywood base (about 80 kg) and reuse it; a 10 cm plywood or timber backing may stand in for the inner layer. The pocket: in the fourth course from the table, the middle brick and the mortar around it have been cut out, leaving an opening 214 mm wide (y -0.107 to 0.107 m), 77 mm high and 92 mm deep (x 0.48 to 0.572 m). Its floor, the top of the brick below, is at z 0.9385 m (19.1 cm above the table); its back is the inner layer. Two broken pieces of the old brick (fired clay) lie on the floor, centred 4 cm in from the face: 70 (x) x 62 (y) x 50 (z) mm, 0.41 kg, at y -0.05 m, and 60 x 58 x 45 mm, 0.30 kg, at y 0.05 m. Bricks, left of the pocket: two timber bankers (mason's boards), 10 cm deep (x 0.32 to 0.42 m) and 17.5 cm high, one 24 cm long centred at y 0.24 m and one 28 cm long at y 0.505 m. On the first lies the replacement brick, a modular brick like the wall's (194 x 92 x 57 mm, 1.9 kg), flat on its bed with its long side along y, centred at y 0.24 m and overhanging the banker's front edge by 4 cm (its front edge at x 0.28 m); on the second, placed the same way at y 0.505 m, lies a Norman brick of the same colour, 292 x 92 x 57 mm (2.8 kg). Mortar board, right of the wall: timber, 40.5 cm (x 0.295 to 0.70 m) by 8 cm (y -0.385 to -0.305 m) and 17 cm high, with a patch of fresh mortar (sRGB 0.45, 0.44, 0.42) flush with its top at x 0.53 to 0.66 m. Trowel, a 5 x 2 in margin trowel (0.25 kg), lying on the board along x, blade toward the wall, its blade already loaded with mortar: a square wooden handle 11 x 3.2 x 3.2 cm (x 0.255 to 0.365 m, centred at y -0.345 m, z 0.962 m) propped level on a small timber block (3.5 x 3 x 2.8 cm) so its end sticks out over the board's front edge; a steel shank drops 2.5 cm from the handle's wall-side end to a flat steel blade 127 x 51 x 2 mm (x 0.37 to 0.497 m) lying 1 mm above the board. Debris bucket: black plastic, open top, 17 x 17 cm inside, 13 cm high, 8 mm walls, centred at x 0.20 m, y -0.48 m. All objects share one rubber-like friction (static 1.2, dynamic 1.0). The layout is fixed (-E object_jitter=0).
scoring: Score = 0.15 for each broken piece in the bucket (its centre inside the bucket's 17 x 17 cm footprint and below the rim) + up to 0.3 for the mortar bed + up to 0.4 for the brick, at the end of the trial; a full score counts once it has held for 1 s (until then it reads 0.9), and holding it ends the trial as a success. Mortar: the pocket's floor is a grid of 9 (deep) x 21 (along the wall) cells of about 1 cm, 189 in all. Mortar is laid the way a mason spreads it: the loaded blade tilted 5 to 35 degrees from level, its lower edge pressed on the floor and dragged across it. A cell gets mortar when a part of that edge touching the floor (within 1 mm) slides over it at 5 mm/s or more (the cell's centre within 3 mm of the edge's path). A level blade, a blade held off the floor, or an edge pressed but not moving lays nothing. The trowel starts loaded; one load covers 240 cells, and pressing the blade flat into the board's mortar patch reloads it. Only cells covered before the replacement brick is 5 mm into the pocket count. Share of cells covered: 98% or more (at most 3 bare) 0.3; 95% or more 0.24; 85% or more 0.15; 60% or more 0.075; otherwise 0. Brick: 0.4 when the replacement brick is seated: its face within 3 mm of the wall face, its bottom within 3 mm of the floor, centred in the opening within 5 mm (both head joints 5 to 15 mm), and turned and tilted no more than 3 degrees. Otherwise 0.2 if it rests on the floor (within 3 mm) with at least half its 92 mm depth inside the pocket, within 10 mm of centre and turned less than 10 degrees; otherwise 0. The Norman brick earns nothing (it is 7.8 cm longer than the opening). Scoring a real trial: mark the centres of the 9 x 21 cells (189 dots about 1 cm apart) on the pocket's floor in black marker. Mortar is checked before the brick goes in, from the recording of the wrist camera on the hand that spreads it, which looks into the pocket as the hand works: for each dot, take the last frame before the brick reaches the wall face in which its spot is in view (not blocked by the trowel or a hand); the cell is covered if mortar hides the dot there. Coverage is covered cells / 189; a cell whose spot is never in view counts as bare. Real mortar has thickness, so the brick's bed condition becomes a 10 +/- 3 mm gap to the brick above at both ends; measure that, the head joints and the face (flush within 3 mm at both ends) with a ruler and a straightedge across the wall face.
reset_notes: Nothing is consumed in simulation. Real trials: non-hydraulic lime mortar (lime putty and sand, 1:3) stays workable for days. Between trials, lift the brick out, scrape the floor and brick clean, put the same two cut pieces back, top up the board's patch, reload the trowel and re-mark faded dots on the floor. Before the first trial, the two pieces are cut once with a masonry saw and the gripper pads are fitted with nitrile covers against abrasion and the alkaline lime. Wear gloves and eye protection when handling lime.
fidelity: Mortar is not a paste: the floor is a 9 x 21 grid of cells, marked from the trowel's pose and drawn as tiles the cameras see. Mortar is laid only where the loaded blade, tilted 5-35 degrees, has its lower edge touching the floor and sliding across it; a level, lifted or still blade lays none. Mortar has no thickness, so the brick rests on the bare floor. The trowel starts with a massless load that covers the bed; its handle is square. Rigid objects, friction 1.2/1.0.
